#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS)
Description: The Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) is a national survey panel by the U.S. Census Bureau (Census). The purpose of the panel is to collect information on topics such as food and nutrition, transportation, employment, and education and to gather data that can be used to improve and inform future surveys. The panel will consist of individuals and households living across the U.S. who have agreed to be contacted and invited to participate in surveys.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS)
Description: The Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) is a national survey panel by the U.S. Census Bureau (Census). The purpose of the panel is to collect information on topics such as food and nutrition, transportation, employment, and education and to gather data that can be used to improve and inform future surveys. The panel will consist of individuals and households living across the U.S. who have agreed to be contacted and invited to participate in surveys.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) comprehensively. Let me start with several searches.I have a solid base. Now let me dig into the methodology documents, the history (HPS→HTOPS transition), and the data access details.I now have the OMB/Paperwork Reduction Act history. Let me dig into the data access channels, partner agencies, and the survey's lineage (Household Pulse Survey and Census Household Panel).I have deep coverage now. Let me fill remaining gaps: the Census Household Panel lineage, the March 2026 design change, and data access channels (interactive tool, PUFs).# Research Report: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS)

**Verification note up front:** Your dataset description is substantially accurate, but it is slightly out of date in one respect. When HTOPS launched in January 2025 it was indeed a *longitudinal panel* of households recruited across the U.S. However, **beginning in March 2026 the Census Bureau transitioned HTOPS from a longitudinal panel back to a cross-sectional design** with independent bi-monthly samples. The "survey panel" framing reflects the 2025 design; current documentation describes it as a national bi-monthly survey. Everything else you provided (publisher, purpose, topics, URL) checks out. Details and sources below.

---

## 1. Identification and Current Status

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) |
| **Publisher** | U.S. Census Bureau (U.S. Department of Commerce), Demographic Programs — part of the **High-Frequency Surveys Program** |
| **Product classification** | **Experimental data product** (Census Bureau's Experimental Data Products portfolio) |
| **Program landing page** | https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html |
| **Data access hub** | https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/household-pulse-survey/data.html (HTOPS data are published under the Household Pulse Survey program pages) |
| **Cadence** | Every other month (bi-monthly collections), each collection ~2–3 weeks in the field |
| **Geography** | National; since March 2026 also the 4 Census regions and the 10 largest CBSAs/MSAs (during 2025's longitudinal phase, releases were national-level only) |
| **Contact** | 1-888-595-1334 (Mon–Fri, 8am–5pm ET); addp.htops@census.gov |
| **Status (as of late 2026)** | Active. Latest releases: March 2026 PUF and tables (re-issued Sept 24, 2026 with revised weights), May 2026, July 2026 (collected July 15–Aug 3, 2026); September and November 2026 collections scheduled |

---

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Statutory authority:** Conducted under **13 U.S.C. §§ 131, 141, 182, 193, and 196** (the Census Bureau's general authority to conduct surveys and collect statistics on the population). (The program page cites these five sections; some pages cite only §§ 141, 182, 193.)
- **Confidentiality:** All responses are protected under the confidentiality provisions of **Title 13, U.S.C.** Participation is **voluntary**.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** OMB Control Number **0607-1029**, under the collection title *"High-Frequency Surveys Program/Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey."* The program page displays an expiration of **09/30/2028**; Reginfo.gov shows the current ICR expiring **07/31/2029**.
- **Clearance history** (from Federal Register notices):
  - July 22, 2024 — OMB cleared Phase 4.2 of the Household Pulse Survey under 0607-1029.
  - **January 15, 2025 — OMB approved the HTOPS recruitment operation plus January and February 2025 topical operations** (this is the survey's founding clearance).
  - April 11, 2025 (Mar/Apr/May collections); June 16, 2025 (Jun/Aug); September 24, 2025 (Sep/Oct/Dec 2025); March 12, 2026 (Mar/May 2026); July/Sep/Nov 2026 collections cleared (latest non-substantive change approved Sept 1, 2026).
- **Public comment:** Notices published in the Federal Register on Dec 9, 2024 (89 FR 97582), Feb 28, 2025 (90 FR 10879), May 13, 2025 (90 FR 20272), Aug 20, 2025 (90 FR 40560), Feb 9, 2026 (91 FR 5705), and June 4, 2026 — **no substantive public comments were received**.
- **Burden accounting:** ~162,768 responses annually; 20 minutes average per response (0.333 hours); **54,202 annual burden hours**; zero cost burden to respondents.
- **Disclosure review:** Products reviewed by the Census Bureau Disclosure Review Board (e.g., for the July 2026 release: Project No. P-7536034, DRB approvals CBDRB-FY26-0334 and CBDRB-FY26-0351).

---

## 3. History and Lineage

HTOPS is the third iteration of a COVID-era innovation, and its history matters enormously for interpreting the time series:

1. **Household Pulse Survey (HPS), April 2020 – September 2024.** Conceived March 23, 2020 and fielded by April 23, 2020, HPS was an interagency "rapid response" survey measuring the social and economic impact of COVID-19 (employment, stimulus spending, food security, housing, education disruption, physical/mental health). Data first released May 20, 2020 — six weeks from concept to release. Originally OMB 0607-1013, later 0607-1029. It ran continuously as a **cross-sectional** survey through Phase 4.2, ending September 16, 2024, with final release October 3, 2024.
2. **Census Household Panel (CHP), ~2022–2024.** A separate longitudinal probability panel (OMB 0607-1025) with rotating "topical operations" — the vehicle for flexible content development. (Its 10th–12th topical operations were cleared July 12, 2024.)
3. **HTOPS, January 2025 – present.** In early October 2024, HPS content transitioned to a longitudinal design, and **in January 2025 HPS and CHP were merged/relaunched as HTOPS** under the High-Frequency Surveys Program. Content alternated bi-monthly between (a) HPS-style timely topical content and (b) content from internal Census partners and stakeholders.
4. **Design change, March 2026.** HTOPS shifted from the longitudinal panel back to a **cross-sectional design** with independent bi-monthly samples of ~136,000 housing units drawn fresh each wave. Census says this supports estimates meeting the quality standards of federal statistical agencies and OMB, and covers the nation, four Census regions, and the 10 largest metro areas.
5. Note the operational gaps: no collection in July 2025 (system updates) and the September 2026 wave includes a methodological test of three internet self-response login methods.

**Practical consequence for data users:** there are effectively three distinct data regimes — 2020–2024 cross-sectional HPS, 2025 longitudinal HTOPS, and 2026+ cross-sectional HTOPS — and trend comparisons across regime boundaries are not straightforward.

---

## 4. Partners and Funders

The Census Bureau is the primary sponsor, but HTOPS is a **multi-agency collaborative**, with partner agencies supplying content and (potentially) funding. Partners named in the source-and-accuracy statements (2025–2026 collections) include:

- **Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)**
- **Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS)**
- **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)**, incl. NCHS, NCIRD, and NIOSH
- **Department of Defense (DOD)**
- **Energy Information Administration (EIA)**
- **Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)**
- **Food and Drug Administration (FDA)**
- **HHS** components: Administration for Community Living (ACL), Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE), Office of the Surgeon General (OSG), Maternal and Child Health Bureau (MCHB)
- **National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)**
- **National Endowment for the Arts (NEA)**
- **USDA Economic Research Service (ERS)** and **Food and Nutrition Service (FNS)**
- **White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA)** (the earlier HPS also worked with CFPB, HHS, the Domestic Policy Council, and even the U.S. Secret Service on content coordination)

---

## 5. Methodology (What a Data Scientist Needs to Know)

- **Sample frame:** Census Bureau **Master Address File (MAF)** — a rigorous, maintained address frame, linkable to Census-curated administrative records.
- **Mode:** Mail invitations; primary response via **internet self-response** on CENTURION (Census's secure web collection platform), with in-bound **CATI** for those who won't respond online; outbound telephone follow-up in the 2026+ design.
- **Instrument:** ~20-minute questionnaire; content combines **core topics** (recurring) and **rotating/topical modules** contributed by partner agencies.
- **Sample size and response:** ~136,000 housing units per wave (2026 design); e.g., July 2026: 136,094 sampled, **12,755 respondents (~9.4% response rate)** — the sample was sized assuming a 10% response rate and targeting a 9% coefficient of variation for a 15% prevalence estimate in each Census region and the 10 largest CBSAs.
- **Weighting:** Survey weights plus **replicate weights** (successive-difference-style) accompany each PUF; population controls matter — see the caution below.
- **Topics covered** (illustrative, across waves): employment status and loss of employment income, use of **AI for work**, unemployment insurance, food sufficiency/food security, housing security and difficulty paying expenses, **energy expenses**, transportation and gas-cost behavior, education/K-12 enrollment, childcare, access to infant formula, health insurance (incl. Medicaid), vaccinations, mental health, suicidal ideation, Narcan use, disability, **social connectedness/social isolation**, trust in government and health information, community and civic engagement, arts participation, natural disasters and extreme heat, dietary guidelines/consumer behavior.

**Known quality issues to track (from official User Notes):**
- The **March 2026 PUF and data tables were re-released September 24, 2026** because the original weights used county-level residential population controls that included Group Quarters, which HTOPS does not cover. If you downloaded March 2026 data before then, you have the wrong weights.
- As an **experimental product**, HTOPS doesn't carry the full quality guarantees of standard federal statistics; Census has also published HPS nonresponse bias analyses (the low ~6–10% response rates historically required heavy weighting).

---

## 6. Data Products and Access (For Data Librarians & Preservationists)

All products are **free and public**:

1. **Public Use Files (PUFs)** — microdata per collection, with a data dictionary and **replicate weight files**; distributed in **CSV and SAS** formats (~10–14 MB), hosted under the HPS "Data → Datasets" pages and ultimately at www2.census.gov. Naming convention: "HTOPS Household Pulse *Month Year* PUF," and topical modules follow a **YYMM convention** (e.g., March 2026 = "HTOPS HPS 2603"; July 2026 = 2607).
2. **Data tables** — detailed estimate tables and standard error tables per collection (e.g., https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2026/demo/hhp/2607.html), sometimes with accompanying infographics (e.g., July 2026 arts and entertainment).
3. **Technical documentation** — per-wave **Source of the Data and Accuracy statements** (PDFs at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/technical-documentation/hhp/), questionnaires for every wave (including historical HPS questionnaires), **User Notes** (an erratum/revision channel — critical for preservation), methodology pages, and subject definitions.
4. **Press releases and blog posts** (e.g., "New Data Tables Released From HTOPS," July 23, 2026).

**Preservation considerations:**
- Because it is an *experimental* product, HTOPS has **no statutory guarantee of continuity** — it exists at the agency's discretion under a rolling PRA clearance, and its design has already changed twice. Archiving each wave's PUF, dictionary, questionnaire, and Source & Accuracy statement as it is released is advisable (the User Notes system means files are **replaced/reposted** — the March 2026 PUF is a live example — so capture dates matter).
- HTOPS/HPS microdata are **not** distributed through the standard data.census.gov/API channel; they live on program web pages and www2.census.gov FTP-style directories.
- The deep lineage (HPS 2020–2024 waves under 0607-1013/0607-1029, CHP under 0607-1025) is documented mainly in Federal Register notices and old technical documentation — worth harvesting for a complete archival record of the series.

---

## 7. Typical Users

Per the Federal Register supporting statements, intended users are: **federal, state, and local agencies; academic and non-government organizations; the media; and the general public.** In practice:

- **Federal policymakers and program agencies** (USDA/FNS nutrition programs, HHS/ASPE health policy, HUD housing, BLS labor market analysts) use it for near-real-time situational awareness between benchmark survey releases — a role it has played since the COVID response era.
- **Economists and researchers** tracking inflation anxiety, spending difficulty, and household well-being at high frequency.
- **Public health researchers** (mental health, social isolation, vaccine uptake — NCHS has published analyses off this infrastructure).
- **Journalists and think tanks** producing timely reporting on household economic stress.
- **Census Bureau itself** — an explicit purpose is **content and methods R&D**: testing question wording, instrumentation, and methods to improve future Census and household surveys, including research supporting the decennial census (successor to the Census Barriers, Attitudes and Motivators Survey role) and the 2026 login-method experiment.

---

## 8. Benefits to the Public

- **Speed:** Near-real-time (weeks, not years) national statistics on emergent social and economic conditions — the founding rationale demonstrated during COVID, when traditional surveys could not move.
- **Breadth with low burden:** A single 20-minute bi-monthly vehicle consolidating content needs of ~19 federal offices, reducing duplicated surveys and respondent burden government-wide.
- **Openness:** Free public microdata with replicate weights and full documentation lets anyone do custom analysis, not just pre-made tables.
- **Policy responsiveness:** Data directly informed federal/state pandemic actions historically and continue to inform responses to food insecurity, housing stress, mental health, energy costs, and disasters.
- **Innovation spillover:** It functions as a testbed for survey methods (web-first collection, MAF-based address sampling, administrative-record linkage) that improve the wider federal statistical system.
- **Design for representativeness:** MAF-based probability sampling with CATI follow-up — a higher-quality alternative to opt-in online panels commonly used for "fast" public opinion data.

---

## 9. Cautions and Caveats Summary

1. **Experimental status** — subject to change or discontinuation; estimates may not meet all federal statistical quality standards (though the 2026 redesign explicitly targets OMB quality standards).
2. **Low response rates (~9–10%)** — heavy reliance on weighting; consult the Source & Accuracy statements and HPS nonresponse bias analyses.
3. **Three incompatible design eras** (2020–24 cross-sectional HPS; 2025 longitudinal HTOPS; 2026+ cross-sectional HTOPS with different geography and weighting).
4. **Reposted/revised files** — check User Notes before citing (e.g., the September 2026 reweighting of March 2026 data).
5. **Limited geography** in the 2025 era (national only); 2026+ adds regions and top-10 metros but still no state-level estimates (unlike the old HPS, which produced state and 15-largest-MSA estimates).
6. **Title 13 confidentiality** — no direct identifiers in PUFs; disclosure-avoidance reviewed.

**Key primary sources:** census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html; the HPS program's Data, Technical Documentation, and User Notes pages; Federal Register notices (esp. 89 FR 97582; 90 FR 20272; the June 4, 2026 notice); reginfo.gov ICR records for 0607-1029; and per-wave Source and Accuracy statements at www2.census.gov.

Let me check the federal staffing tracker, HTOPS-specific user notes/alterations, and the government shutdown impact on releases.# HTOPS Dataset Risk Assessment

**Assessment date:** October 2026. This assessment builds on the prior research report with additional research into agency staffing, budget, policy actions, and HTOPS-specific operational record.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- All prior-cycle data remain publicly posted: the HPS datasets pages list every PUF, replicate weight file, and data dictionary from 2020 through 2025, and 2026 collections to date, on census.gov and www2.census.gov (census.gov/data/datasets/time-series/demo/hhp/2025.html, /2026.html).
- Questionnaires, Source and Accuracy statements, and User Notes for all waves back to April 2020 remain accessible, including a full historical User Notes archive (census.gov/programs-surveys/household-pulse-survey/technical-documentation/user-notes.2026.html).
- The one known content gap — the February 2025 PUF "omitted select variables" — was remediated by Census publishing a free-standing Supplemental File in SAS and CSV, so no data elements are actually inaccessible (2025 datasets page).
- No evidence of removal of HPS/HTOPS data files from Census servers. (A related but distinct removal: CDC pages using HPS long COVID data were removed during the 2025 online-resource purges — Wikipedia's tracker of Trump administration resource removals — but that affected CDC's analytical products, not the Census Bureau's underlying survey files.)

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:** The February 2025 PUF did ship with omitted variables (fixed by supplemental file); the March and May 2026 PUFs were *replaced* with corrected weights on September 10, 2026, so anyone who archived the original files holds data Census now considers erroneous.

**Verdict: No Known Issue.** The full historical record (2020–present) remains available from the primary source, and the known file defects were corrected or remediated rather than papered over. The main preservation hazard is silent file replacement (superseded versions not retained), which is a documentation practice issue rather than a removal.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The ICR (OMB No. 0607-1029) is active and has been renewed repeatedly before expiration — most recent non-substantive change approved September 1, 2026; current clearance runs through 2028–2029 (reginfo.gov; program page).
- Collections continue on the bi-monthly schedule: July 2026 data (collected July 15–Aug 3) was released September 10, 2026; September and November 2026 collections were OMB-cleared (Federal Register notice of June 4, 2026, 2026-11172).
- The March 2026 redesign actually *expanded* the sample (~136,000 housing units per wave, up from ~30,000 panel members) and added subnational estimates.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The April 2025 release was delayed — the American Statistical Association's *The Nation's Data at Risk: 2025* report explicitly lists "Census Bureau: Household Pulse Survey for April not yet released" under Product Delays, amid the 2025 turbulence.
- The October–December 2025 government shutdown disrupted Census release schedules agency-wide (ASA report; multiple products delayed).
- The March and May 2026 PUFs required re-release with corrected weights on September 10, 2026 — a roughly three-to-five-month lag in publishing *correct* data (User Note, 2603_HTOPS...09102026.pdf).
- The program skipped/restructured collections during the 2024–2025 design transitions (cross-sectional → longitudinal → back to cross-sectional), leaving gaps and discontinuities in the series.

**Evidence for High Risk:** One could argue a skipped collection (HPS-content releases appeared only in February, April, and June 2025 on the HPS pages, with the next HPS-content release not until March 2026), but the underlying HTOPS program continued collecting in the intervening months under non-HPS topical modules, so this is a publication-scope artifact of the design rather than a terminated collection.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** The ICR is current and collections are proceeding, but the record since January 2025 shows real publication delays (April 2025, shutdown effects) and materially corrected re-releases (March/May 2026) — matching "typical or intended publication date missed and/or publication delayed."

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** The 2026 redesign explicitly aims to meet OMB/federal statistical quality standards, enlarged the sample, and added subnational detail (4 Census regions + 10 largest metros) that the 2025 design lacked.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The March and May 2026 PUFs were published with misaligned population controls (county residential controls including Group Quarters that HTOPS doesn't sample) and had to be re-weighted — a realized accuracy failure, though corrected (User Note, Sept. 10, 2026).
- Response rates are very low (~9.4% in July 2026; sample sized assuming 10%), requiring heavy weighting and raising nonresponse-bias concerns; the product remains classified as *experimental* and "may not meet some of the Census Bureau's statistical quality standards" (experimental data products page).
- ASA's 2025 report flags agency-wide quality degradation risks (e.g., ABS sample cuts, CPI collection suspensions), indicating an environment where quality resources are stretched.

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- The 2025 longitudinal phase produced national-level estimates only — a reduction in geographic granularity relative to the pre-2024 HPS (which published state and 15-largest-MSA estimates), and the 2026 design still does not restore state-level detail.
- Timeliness reductions occurred: HPS moved from roughly continuous/monthly collection (2020–2024) to bi-monthly; the April 2025 release was late; March 2026 corrected data wasn't available until September 2026.
- Three design regimes in three years (cross-sectional → longitudinal → cross-sectional) break series comparability.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** The 2026 redesign arrested the granularity and timeliness slide (bigger sample, subnational estimates, target of OMB quality standards), so the trajectory is stable-to-improving. But the realized weighting error, ~9% response rates, experimental status, and unresolved loss of state-level estimates constitute genuine, ongoing — not merely potential — quality concerns. If the March 2026 re-release is weighted heavily, a case for High exists; I judge the corrections and redesign to be genuine remediation, so Moderate.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- HTOPS is **not statutorily mandated**. It operates under the Census Bureau's general Title 13 authority (13 U.S.C. 131, 141, 182, 193, 196), not under any statute naming the survey, its topics, or a publication requirement — unlike the decennial census, ACS, or CPS. It is a discretionary "experimental data product."
- The FY2026 Census budget narrative states that "By the end of fiscal 2026, the Census Bureau will have eliminated functions that are not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" (GovExec; The Census Project) — language that directly implicates a non-mandated experimental survey.
- Partial substitutes exist for content areas (ACS, CPS, NHIS cover food security, employment, health topics), though none replicate the high-frequency, rapid-deployment function.

**Evidence for Moderate/No Known Issue (mitigating):**
- The Title 13 authority cited is standard and not vague; the survey has clear, documented programmatic use by ~19 federal partners (BLS, CDC/NCHS, USDA ERS/FNS, HUD, HHS/ASPE, NCES, etc.) and an explicit methodological R&D role supporting decennial census planning.
- No other federal collection can serve the near-real-time pulse function, so it is not redundant.

**Verdict: High Risk.** On this rubric's own terms, HTOPS sits in the High cell: authorization is general rather than explicit, it is not required for implementation of any statute or program, and topic-level alternatives exist. The administration's stated intent to eliminate non-statutory functions makes this vulnerability concrete, even though HTOPS has so far survived the triage.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **1,000+ staff lost:** ~1,300 Census Bureau employees took deferred resignations, voluntary separations, or early retirements in 2025 (Johnny Zuagar, president, AFGE Census Council 241, via AP News).
- **15–19% workforce decline:** ASA estimates a 15% staffing loss since FY24; GAO found a 16% decline (13,312 → 11,119) between January 20 and October 22, 2025; OPM-covered employment fell 19.1% (13,306 → 10,764) from January 2025 to June 2026 (federalhiringdata.com; ASA 2026 Midyear Update).
- **Leadership removed/unstable:** Director Robert Santos resigned February 14, 2025 mid-term; career Deputy Director Ron Jarmin served only in an acting capacity; in September 2025 the administration installed Trump appointee George Cook — a Commerce political staffer also serving as acting undersecretary — as acting director, a move census experts characterized as raising "alarm bells" (AP; NPR; CRS IF11845). The bureau's leadership roster showed 18 vacancies at the top (AP News).
- **Program-level budget cut:** the FY2026 enacted appropriation cut the Current Surveys and Programs account (which houses demographic survey operations) by ~$40 million / 12.3% vs. FY25 (CRS IF12714; The Census Project).

**Evidence for Moderate/No Known Issue (mitigating):**
- The Census Bureau's *overall* FY2026 enacted budget is $1.490 billion — a $108 million *increase* over FY24/FY25 (CRS IF13105) — as Congress prioritized 2030 Census preparation.
- No division-specific elimination of the Demographic Programs/High-Frequency Surveys staff has been reported; HTOPS operations continued through 2026.

**Verdict: High Risk.** Two independent rubric triggers for High are met (1,000+ staff lost; leadership removed/changed), with a third partially met (a >10% cut to the relevant program account). Only the agency-wide topline increase keeps this from being worse.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **DOGE terminations at the same agency:** In spring 2025, the Department of Government Efficiency announced it had "terminated" five Census Bureau surveys (~$16.5M) conducted for other agencies (likely including the Survey of Inmates in Local Jails and the DOD Ask U.S. Panel), and said remaining surveys were under a "one-by-one" review (AP News). HTOPS shares the key vulnerability profile of the terminated surveys: non-mandated, experimental, and partly reimbursable/partner-funded — and several of its partner agencies (e.g., DOD) were themselves cut.
- **Explicit administration policy to cut non-mandated functions:** FY2026 budget documents commit to eliminating functions "not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" by end of FY2026 (GovExec; The Census Project).
- **Leadership politicization:** installation of a political loyalist as acting director without the statistical-management qualifications normally expected (NPR, Sept. 2025).
- **Adjacent removals:** the broader 2025 online-resource removals included HPS-adjacent content (CDC's long-COVID pages built on HPS data), and SOGI questions were stripped from multiple federal surveys (ASA 2025 report) — demonstrating willingness to alter survey content and withdraw published data products government-wide.
- **Proposed statistical-agency reorganization:** the FY2026 budget supports reorganizing BLS, BEA, and Census under Commerce (The Census Project), which could restructure or relocate HTOPS's institutional home.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- No administration statement, executive order, or budget line has named HTOPS for elimination or alteration; the DOGE cuts hit *reimbursable* surveys for other departments, whereas HTOPS is a Census-led program with a broad interagency constituency.
- HTOPS has demonstrably thrived post-January 2025: launched on schedule, expanded to ~30,000 households in April 2025, redesigned with a larger sample in March 2026, ICR renewals obtained without substantive public objection through September 2026.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** Not supportable — the policy environment at the parent agency has changed materially since January 2025 (terminations of other surveys, leadership change, non-mandate elimination directive), and several HTOPS content areas (health, food security, equity-adjacent topics) sit near politically contested territory.

**Verdict: High Risk.** HTOPS itself has not been directly targeted and remains in operation, but the rubric's "other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities" has clearly occurred at the agency level, and the administration's stated framework — eliminating non-statutory functions and reviewing surveys "one-by-one" — categorically threatens a voluntary, experimental, non-mandated survey like HTOPS. Its survival so far appears to reflect its utility and interagency sponsorship rather than any policy protection.

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Level |
|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Future Data Availability | **Moderate Risk** |
| Data Quality | **Moderate Risk** |
| Statutory Context | **High Risk** |
| Staffing and Funding | **High Risk** |
| Policy | **High Risk** |

**Overall read:** The data itself is, so far, unusually well-preserved — every file since 2020 remains downloadable, and collections are proceeding on an active ICR. The structural vulnerabilities are institutional: HTOPS is a discretionary experimental program with no statutory floor, housed in an agency that has lost ~15–19% of its staff and its Senate-confirmed leadership, operating under an administration that has already terminated comparable surveys and has formally committed to eliminating non-mandated functions. For a preservationist, the practical implications are: (1) archive each wave's PUF, dictionary, questionnaire, and Source & Accuracy statement at release time, since Census replaces defective files rather than versioning them (the March/May 2026 re-weighting proves silent supersession happens); and (2) treat continuity beyond the current ICR window (2028/2029) as genuinely uncertain.
